title: Delegate the outcome, not the method
body: Tell people what "done" looks like and by when, then let them choose how to get there. Prescribing every step turns skilled people into order-takers.

title: Grove's rule of manager output
body: Andy Grove's core idea in High Output Management: a manager's output is not their personal work, it is the output of the team and the neighboring teams they influence. Optimize for that number, not your own to-do list.

title: The drifted handoff
body: You handed off a project last month. The result has drifted from the approach you would have taken. What now?

options.label: Take it back and redo it your way
Judge it against whether it meets the actual goal, not your original method
Correct the approach in front of the team
Say nothing and hope it works out

explanation: Delegation means giving up the method along with the task. If the outcome meets the goal, a different path is a feature of delegation, not a bug.

title: The reversed decision
body: A manager let their lead decide the launch date, then overturned it in a public channel two days later. Within a month, every decision — however small — was routed back to the manager for approval. Reversing a delegated call in public costs more than a slightly worse decision ever would.

title: Hand off one thing
body: Pick one recurring task that only you currently do. Write down the decision criteria you use for it, and hand the task to someone else this week.

title: Trust is a loop, not a leap
body: Start with a small delegation, give honest feedback on how it went, then widen the scope. Handing over something huge with no track record sets both of you up to fail.

title: Ask what they need before you ask why
body: Before asking 'why isn't this done,' ask 'what do you need from me?' Most delegation failures are missing context or a blocked dependency, not a lack of effort.

title: Write a one-page delegation brief
body: For the next thing you hand off, write one page: the goal, the constraints, who has decision rights, and the check-in cadence. No more than that — the rest is theirs to figure out.

title: Delegate the whole problem, not the leftover 80%
body: Keeping the interesting 20% — the key design call, the stakeholder conversation — and handing off only the execution is not delegation, it is outsourcing busywork. And it caps how much the other person can grow.

title: The handoff that was never really handed off
body: A manager delegated a project but stayed cc'd on every thread and jumped into decisions. The person stopped deciding anything — they just forwarded things up. Visible hovering undoes a delegation faster than any words ever could.

title: Match the ask to their next level, not your comfort
body: Delegating slightly past someone's current ability — with support available — builds capability faster than delegating safely within it.

title: Stuck and silent
body: You delegated a task to someone who's now stuck and hasn't asked for help in several days. What's the first move?

options.label: Wait longer — they will figure it out
Check in directly and ask where they're stuck, without taking the task back yet
Quietly reassign it to someone else

explanation: Most people under-ask for help far more than they over-ask. A direct, low-stakes check-in usually unblocks the work without undermining their ownership of it.

title: Give away the credit before you give away the task
body: Publicly naming who now owns something, and why you trust them with it, makes the handoff real to the rest of the team — not just to the person receiving it.

title: Hand over a decision you're still making for someone
body: Identify a decision you keep making for someone who's actually ready to make it themselves. Tell them explicitly: "this one's yours now."

title: A delegation without a deadline is a suggestion
body: Pair every handoff with a specific check-in date, or it will quietly slip to the bottom of both your priority lists.
